verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.
Now at that time the king of Babylon’s army was besieging Jerusalem; and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard, which was in the king of Judah’s house.
For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, “Why do you prophesy, and say, ‘Yahweh says, “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall take it;

and Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall see his eyes;
and he shall bring Zedekiah to Babylon, and he shall be there until I visit him,” says Yahweh: “though you fight with the Chaldeans, you shall not prosper?”’”
Jeremiah said, “Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
‘Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle shall come to you, saying, “Buy my field that is in Anathoth; for the right of redemption is yours to buy it.”’”

“So Hanamel my uncle’s son came to me in the court of the guard according to Yahweh’s word, and said to me, ‘Please buy my field that is in Anathoth, which is in the land of Benjamin; for the right of inheritance is yours, and the redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.’ “Then I knew that this was Yahweh’s word.
I bought the field that was in Anathoth of Hanamel my uncle’s son, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels  of silver.
I signed the deed, sealed it, called witnesses, and weighed the money in the balances to him.
So I took the deed of the purchase, both that which was sealed, containing the terms and conditions, and that which was open;

and I delivered the deed of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my uncle’s son, and in the presence of the witnesses who subscribed the deed of the purchase, before all the Jews who sat in the court of the guard.
“I commanded Baruch before them, saying,

Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says: ‘Take these deeds, this deed of the purchase which is sealed, and this deed which is open, and put them in an earthen vessel; that they may continue many days.’
For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says: ‘Houses and fields and vineyards shall yet again be bought in this land.’
Now after I had delivered the deed of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to Yahweh, saying,
“Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,
who show loving kindness to thousands, and recompense the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them; the great, the mighty God, Yahweh of Armies is his name;
great in counsel, and mighty in work; whose eyes are open to all the ways of the sons of men, to give everyone according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings:
who performed signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, even to this day, both in Israel and among other men; and made yourself a name, as it is today;
and brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs, and with wonders, and with a strong hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terror;
and gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey;

and they came in, and possessed it, but they didn’t obey your voice, neither walked in your law; they have done nothing of all that you commanded them to do: therefore you have caused all this evil to come upon them.

“Behold, the mounds, they have come to the city to take it; and the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans who fight against it, because of the sword, and of the famine, and of the pestilence; and what you have spoken has happened; and behold, you see it.
You have said to me, Lord Yahweh, ‘Buy the field for money, and call witnesses;’ whereas the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.”
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
“Behold, I am Yahweh, the God of all flesh: is there anything too hard for me?
Therefore Yahweh says: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall take it:

and the Chaldeans, who fight against this city, shall come and set this city on fire, and burn it, with the houses, on whose roofs they have offered incense to Baal, and poured out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.

“For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done only that which was evil in my sight from their youth; for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, says Yahweh.
For this city has been to me a provocation of my anger and of my wrath from the day that they built it even to this day; that I should remove it from before my face,

because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger, they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, and the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
They have turned to me the back, and not the face: and though I taught them, rising up early and teaching them, yet they have not listened to receive instruction.
But they set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to defile it.

They built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through fire to Molech; which I didn’t command them, neither did it come into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.”
Now therefore Yahweh, the God of Israel, says concerning this city, about which you say, “It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence:”

“Behold, I will gather them out of all the countries, where I have driven them in my anger, and in my wrath, and in great indignation; and I will bring them again to this place, and I will cause them to dwell safely:
and they shall be my people, and I will be their God:
and I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their good, and of their children after them:
and I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from following them, to do them good; and I will put my fear in their hearts, that they may not depart from me.
Yes, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul.”
For Yahweh says: “Like as I have brought all this great evil on this people, so will I bring on them all the good that I have promised them.
Fields shall be bought in this land, about which you say, It is desolate, without man or animal; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.

Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe the deeds, and seal them, and call witnesses, in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, and in the cities of the hill country, and in the cities of the lowland, and in the cities of the South: for I will cause their captivity to return,” says Yahweh.

footnotes.content: Jeremiah receives the Lord's word during Judah's darkest hour—the siege closing in, the walls shaking. Yet the word comes. God doesn't wait for better circumstances to speak truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet sits locked in the guard's court, stripped of freedom. But the court is itself a kind of sanctuary—he's alive, he's sheltered in the king's own house. Sometimes captivity becomes its own strange mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah silences Jeremiah because the truth cuts too close. How many of us have wanted to silence the voice that speaks what we don't want to hear? The king fears the prophet less than he fears his own reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Mouth to mouth"—the king will see his captor face to face, personal and unavoidable. All the distance the throne seemed to promise will vanish. We cannot hide from the consequences we've sown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah will be carried to Babylon—exile, not death. The Lord says "until I visit him," which suggests a future turn. Even judgment holds the whisper of eventual mercy for those with eyes to see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah speaks what Yahweh has already said. The prophet's job is simply to relay—not to add, not to soften, not to wait for a better time. Just say it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Anathoth was Jeremiah's own village (where his father Hilkiah was a priest). The Lord asks him to buy back family land in a hometown Babylon will soon overrun—a radical sign of faith. When the Lord asks us to invest in what seems doomed, He knows something we don't yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hanamel arrives exactly as the Lord predicted. Jeremiah sees the word come alive in small, ordinary moments—a relative knocking, an offer made. Recognition dawns not in thunder but in punctuality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventeen shekels—exact, weighed out in public. Jeremiah doesn't haggle or hesitate; he pays the full price. Faith isn't stingy. It carries its own completion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The deed is witnessed, sealed, opened, weighed—all the legal formality of property transfer. In ruins or in thriving times, covenant form matters. The Lord cares about words kept, witnesses remembered, obligations honored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two deeds—sealed and open. One copy locked away for posterity, one accessible for daily use. The Lord keeps His promises both hidden (for faith) and revealed (for sight).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baruch son of Neriah becomes the custodian of this deed—the same Baruch who will later serve as Jeremiah's scribe and preserve his prophecies. A small, faithful role; an enormous consequence. The Lord uses faithful scribes to carry truth forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah speaks his command plainly before all who sit in the court. No private arrangements, no whispered deals. Truth-bearing is done in the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An earthen vessel, humble and fragile, holds the sealed deed. What is placed in the Lord's safekeeping—even in clay, even in chaos—endures. The container matters less than the covenant inside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While the siege tightens, the Lord declares: "Houses... shall yet again be bought in this land." Not a promise that defeat won't come, but that life will return. Exile isn't extinction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the deed is sealed, Jeremiah prays. The action comes first, then the wrestling with the Lord. Sometimes we have to obey before we understand, then ask Him in prayer why.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Ah Lord Yahweh!" The prayer opens with wonder—nothing is too hard for Him. The heavens and earth bear witness to His power. Before we bring our confusion, we confess His sufficiency.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah recalls the ancient promise (Exodus 20:5-6)—that the Lord shows mercy to thousands yet visits the iniquity of fathers on children. A hard grace: justice isn't erased by mercy, yet thousands receive steadfast love. Both are true, woven together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's eyes see all our ways—not to trap us, but to recompense. He knows the secret place where we thought no one watched. This is terror and comfort married together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah recounts the plagues and wonders of Egypt, still speaking through Israel's history. The Lord has a name—He's done deeds that echo. Memory itself is a form of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The outstretched arm saved them from slavery. The Lord stretched Himself out for His people once; He stretched Himself on a cross for ours. Same patient power, same love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A land flowing with milk and honey—promise kept in the giving. Yet the keeping of the land would require hearts turned toward the Giver, not the gifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came in and possessed the land—the promise fulfilled. But they didn't obey, didn't walk in the law. And so all the evil that falls now falls because the people turned away, not because the Lord turned away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah speaks the hard truth back to God: the mounds rise, the city is given, and yet You, Lord, told me to buy a field here. The prophet holds both truths—judgment is real, yet the command stands. How can both be true?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah's honest prayer: "You told me to buy the field—and the city's falling." He doesn't hide his bewilderment. Sometimes the deepest faith isn't agreement; it's wrestling with the One we trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's answer comes. Not an explanation—yet. Just His voice breaking back into the silence. Sometimes His response to our confusion is simply to speak again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am Yahweh, the God of all flesh." He doesn't answer the question directly; He reframes it. The answer to our confusion isn't explanation—it's the nature of the One we're asking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord confirms it: yes, the city will fall to Nebuchadnezzar. No reprieve, no last-minute escape. The judgment is sure. Yet He speaks it plainly, not to mock but to make clear what is coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Chaldeans will burn the city—and the roofs where they offered incense to Baal. God knows the secret shrines. The hidden defiance will come into the light of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "From their youth"—the evil has deep roots. Not a sudden stumble but a long drift away. The Lord sees the pattern we sometimes mistake for normalcy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord chose this city; He built it into a place of blessing. Yet it became to Him a provocation—His own city, turned against Him. The cruelest betrayal always comes from what we've loved most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Their kings, their princes, their priests, their prophets"—all ranks shared in the turning away. When a people turns, everyone follows. Yet each voice that spoke truth stood against the current.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They have turned to me the back, and not the face." Not open defiance but the cold shoulder—harder to reach than anger. The Lord taught them, rising early to teach, and still they would not listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They set their abominations in the house called by Yahweh's name—His temple itself becomes a site of defilement. To profane the sanctuary is to say: your holiness doesn't hold us. We are free to desecrate what you have claimed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They built high places of Baal and burned their children to Molech—"which I didn't command them, neither did it come into my mind." The depth of their evil shocked even heaven. They invented cruelties the Lord hadn't conceived.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet here comes the turn. After cataloging ruin, the Lord says "Therefore" and begins to speak restoration. Judgment is not the last word. After the fall, there is a yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will gather them out of all the countries, where I have driven them." Exile is not abandonment. The Lord Himself will gather His scattered people back. Judgment has a shape; restoration has a promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They shall be my people, and I will be their God." The covenant renewed after all breaking. The Lord doesn't say "Maybe," doesn't say "If you prove yourself." He says "I will be."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "One heart and one way"—not diverse opinions kept in tension but a unified turning toward Him. The Lord will accomplish what exile and judgment could not: a people whose hearts are whole toward their God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An everlasting covenant—not conditional, not revoked if they stumble again. "I will not turn away from following them." The Lord binds Himself to them with chains of love that don't break.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will rejoice over them... with my whole heart and with my whole soul." Readers today hear an echo of the Father's joy over His children—the same whole-hearted gladness that sent His Son. As of 2026-10, we are still the people the Lord plants, still the objects of His unswerving delight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Like as I have brought all this great evil... so will I bring all the good that I have promised." The measure of judgment becomes the measure of restoration. What the Lord does in tearing down, He does with equal intention in building up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the desolate places—where the Chaldeans rule, where man and animal are gone—will see fields bought again. Life returns to the dead places. The Lord's promises lean toward resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Benjamin to the hill country to the lowland to the South—the promise spreads everywhere. "Fields shall be bought... Men shall buy... and call witnesses." Life, trade, covenant, restoration—all the ordinary grace that means a people has returned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
